claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially processed into a high-temperature BCC state.
The stability of the high-temperature BCC phase is governed by a balance between composition-dependent thermodynamic driving force and kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
The relevant thermodynamic driving force can be quantified by the free-energy difference between metastable BCC and more stable low-temperature phases.
Transformation occurs only when the free-energy driving force exceeds a critical threshold and diffusion is sufficiently activated.
Systematically varying annealing temperature and duration while fixing cooling rate controls atomic mobility and changes the thermodynamic driving force.
Low-temperature or very short anneals provide a baseline in which diffusion is negligible.
The emergence and growth of lower-energy phases from the BCC matrix can be tracked through evolving phase fractions.
XRD and electron microscopy can measure the evolving phase fraction and identify incipient nucleation and growth.
At temperatures where composition makes ΔG sufficiently negative, the driving force for transformation increases.
Transformation is delayed until annealing permits enough atomic diffusion to overcome nucleation barriers.
BCC transforms only when thermodynamic instability and diffusion activation coincide.
Annealing above a specific temperature for sufficiently long durations will reproducibly increase the transformed phase fraction.
The transformed equilibrium phase may be FCC or another lower-temperature phase.
Samples annealed at lower temperatures or for insufficient time will largely retain the BCC phase.
Below a joint temperature-time threshold, kinetic limitations preserve BCC even when transformation is thermodynamically favorable.
Above the joint temperature-time threshold, a clear transition in phase fraction occurs.
Minor alloying effects or processing subtleties may shift the transformation boundaries.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis suggests that sufficiently high annealing temperature increases the effective thermodynamic driving force, while the baseline also associates low temperature with retained BCC because of slow diffusion. It does not specify the temperature dependence of ΔG, so the effects of temperature on driving force and kinetics cannot be cleanly distinguished.
